Distinguished colleagues, it's a great pleasure for me to welcome you all to the annual interactive dialogue between members of the International Law Commission and the Sixth Committee. Sweden is honored to co-host this important event together with Austria, continuing our shared commitment to fostering meaningful exchanges between the Commission and the Committee. This dialogue serves a valuable platform for frank and informal exchange between members of ILC and the Sixth Committee on current topics, uh, on the Commission's agenda. It also offers an opportunity to look ahead and reflect on future— on the future direction of the Commission's work. At the outset, allow me to commend the ILC on its work during its 76th session. As we all know, the Commission faced exceptional challenges due to the liquidity crisis affecting the entire United Nations system nonetheless, but despite these constraints, It has made progress on several important key topics. This is a testament to its resilience and commitment. We will begin today's dialogue with a presentation by Mr. Martins Paparinskis, Chair of the 76th Session of the ILC, who will share an overview of the Commission's work at this session. Following this, I will then invite the co-chairs of the Study Group on Sea Level Rise in Relation to International Law, Mrs. Nilüfer Oral, Mr. Juan José Ruda Sanatollaria, and Mrs. Patricia Galvão Teles, to present on the topic of sea level rise in relation to international law, for which, as we all know, the Commission adopted its final report and concluded its consideration. I will also allow for questions and comments between each of these sessions, and I will also try to be a little bit conscious of our time to make sure that we finish at 6 o'clock. But with no further ado, Mr. Paparinskis, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam Moderator. Let me begin by thanking the permanent missions of Sweden and Austria, the co-hosts for the interactive dialogue, and grateful to Madam Theresa Hayden, the moderator. I don't think that you will hear too many smoking gun announcements. Broadly, we have been speaking about what has happened in the International Law Commission 76 session for this week. But let me just summarize in a way that would emphasize the points that struck me and the Commission as the most important. So by way of background, I recall that in Resolution 79/121 of 4 December 2024, the General Assembly decided that the 76th session of the Commission would be held from 14th April to 30th May 2025, and from 30th June to 31st July 2025, and stressed the importance of having a 12-week session for the 76th session of the Commission. On 27th of March 2025, the Commission was formally informed that the budget of the Office of Legal Affairs for 2025 could only allow for sufficient funding to enable the Commission to convene its 76th the session for a duration of 5 weeks. As a result, this session took place from 28th of April to 30th of May. The reduction was unprecedented in the history of the Commission. So just to drive home the point, never in the first 75 years has the Commission met for less than 9 weeks. I note as well that we— decided to also meet on Monday mornings and Friday afternoons, which have been traditionally reserved for the work of the Special Rapporteur on preparation of the commentaries, statements for the drafting committee, as well as for members more generally in the work in the library. So what were the main issues arising from the reduced length of this session? Well, the most basic one is that the Commission's expectations were not met. We originally planned to complete the work on sea level rise in relation to international law, adopt two second reading texts on immunity of state officials and general principles of law, and finalize two first reading texts on subsidiary means and settlement of disputes to which international organizations are parties. And the expectation was to conclude the work on the topic of success session of States in respect of state responsibility and progress on other matters. So, an ambitious programme of work. However, reduction of the time for the consideration of each topic resulted first in the limited ability of members to fully present their views during plenary debate, in line with the recommendation by the Bureau to limit, uh, the plenary statement time and an incomplete debate. And that is something that I'll return to, uh, in the second half of my presentation. Also, unavailability of time for the preparation, translation, and consideration of commentaries to draft provisions led to postponement of adoption of said draft provisions to the 77th session. Namely, immunity of state officials from foreign criminal jurisdiction on second reading, general principles of law on second reading, and subsidiary means for determination of rules of international law on first reading. So I heard rightly states emphasize in their statements the disappointment that commentaries do not accompany the provisions, that is a direct consequence of the reduced length and the one half of the session not providing for the time necessary for the translation of the relevant materials, which is a must of— through the United Nations system. The conclusion of the topic on succession of states in respect of state responsibility was also postponed to the 77th session, and only a single working group meeting was held. Such delay overall has knock-on effects, so there are multiple layers in which that disadvantages the Commission's work. With the two topics initially planned to be concluded on first reading no longer being on track for completion on second reading during the current quinquennium, there was no plenary debate on the topics on settlement of disputes to which international organizations are parties, non-legally binding international agreements, and prevention and repression of piracy and armed robbery at sea. The Commission was only able to dedicate a single meeting each, under the format of a working group, for the consideration of these topics. This measure was taken to allow members to have some preliminary discussions on reports prepared by the special rapporteurs, who are also the the chairs of the respective working groups. So where we are now. So the short point is that the Commission is no longer able to meet the schedule of work presented in the first year of the current quinquennium, and something that the special rapporteurs in particular have been having an eye towards in planning their work. The cumulative loss of 9 weeks, 7 this year— and I recall the 2 weeks lost last year represents the loss of nearly an entire annual session during the current quinquennium. Extension of the cycles of consideration and completion of each topic or its programme of work thereby reverses efficiencies achieved in recent years from improvements to the working methods of the Commission. It also impacts the work of the Sixth Committee, since the Commission's annual report provides less subject matter to sustain the debate during International Law Week. It impacts the relationship of the Commission with other bodies due to the impossibility of scheduling exchanges of views during the session. The Commission was unable to have an exchange of views with the African Union Commission on International Law the Asian-African Legal Consultative Organization, the Committee of Legal Advisers on Public International Law of the Council of Europe, and the Inter-American Juridical Committee. So none of these meetings took place this year, nor, would I add, the previous year, also reflecting the cut in the length of the session. No meetings of the Working Group on Methods of Work and Procedures took place. Owing to an availability of time. So again, that goes to the point I also heard recurring in the statements by states in relation to the issue of improvements in methods. Furthermore, owing to the changes to the scheduling of the Commission, the International Law Seminar could not be convened as per its established practice in July. And exceptionally, its duration had to be reduced from 3 to 2 weeks. The first week of the seminar was scheduled to run concurrently with the last week of the Commission, which resulted in a very intense program for participants. Let me now address the final point, and it is really something that has been raised variously by states, and it was particularly raised by Singapore earlier today, and it was the question of the consideration of remote participation or a variety of virtual ways. And that was something that was considered by the Commission. There were three issues that arose in that consideration. The first was a technological one, which I describe, but it would probably be somebody like Mr. Pronto who would be able to provide further detail and is essentially dismantlement of the system for remote accessibility that had been established during COVID which is of course an unfortunate step backwards. There's also the fact that the members of the Commission are located in different regions of the world, in different time zones, making it challenging to conduct meetings virtually. That is a lesson learned by the institution from the COVID-19 pandemic, when it became clear that effective use of virtual meetings was not possible. And the final point is that the Commission attaches great importance to multilingualism, which is also factored in the challenges of holding meetings virtually, because the The concern is that to the extent that meetings do not place— take place in the normal fashion, there may be a preponderance of the argument taking place in one language rather than five others. That was the last point that I wanted to say. Thank you, Madam Moderator. 9.5 minutes.
Beautiful.

Thank you, Madame Moderator. Well, I mean, I think the points that have been made throughout this week, perhaps Looking at the 77th session, the expectation that General Assembly, through its various committees, would provide sufficient resources for the Commission to be able to carry out its mandate through the Sixth Committee reflected, of course, in deliberations of the relevant documents, appropriate communication of the point with colleagues in other settings, such as the Fifth Committee. So I think that that would probably be the point that the Commission can work with the resources that it has been provided. If there is a mismatch between the mandate that it has to do and the resources that it has to— has been provided with, the mandate will not be fulfilled, or the quality would suffer, and I think that we did try to ensure that the quality of the argument and discussion did not suffer.

Thank you. Thank you, Madam Moderator, and thank you to the Chair of the Commission for your introduction. Thank you, and I thank the distinguished representative of Iceland for her point. I would want to ensure the states that the Bureau and members reflected very deeply on these matters, and many of the points that states have raised in their submissions as possible alternatives were considered. I think Some streamlining-related adjustments were made that I mentioned, sort of, you know, working throughout the full week with the expectation that when work needs to be done, it is done, that there's always time to wake up earlier for the library, shortened plenary statement time, although of course Of course, I think the members of the International Law Commission are also appreciative of the same costs that may happen in different settings. One might circulate a longer written statement, but that would not be reflected in the summary records, and that is important for the long-term ability to trace the development of international law. That to be done properly through the translation of relevant materials and discussions in the six United Nations languages, that it is impossible to have excessive shortcuts. So I think as a starting point, we are also trusting you that you are trying really to find all possible means to make the best possible out of the situation and to work as hard, as robust, as good as possible despite the financial constraints. Your work will progress much better and we will benefit much more if you have two meetings. I think there are three points which you have to bear in mind in that case. I think it's nice to agree on a budget and then not pay the contributions to the UN. There is a general situation that might make it very difficult to go for more, but we are going, and we hope all our partners here and other states also are going to support that there will be a budget for 10 weeks. But there's also a third element, I think, which we also should bear in mind, because While we try to do everything not only to budget but also that the money will be available for 10 meetings next year, we also expect the Commission to fulfill its mandate efficiently and to opt also for cost-effective meetings arrangements. Because there are, depending what kind of meeting arrangements you are choosing, and venue will be one of the important questions there, it will have significant impact on the budget. Thank you so much, and by this we will conclude this part. I am conscious of the questions that are still out there, but allow me nevertheless to carry on with our next topic for this interactive debate. First and foremost, I want to warmly congratulate the study group on the sea level rise in relation to international Law and the three co-chairs that we have here on the final report on the topic and their excellent work on this matter that is of greatest importance for the international community as a whole. Based on the earlier issues papers and additional papers by the co-chairs, the final report of the study group sets out the legal issues in relation to the law of the sea, statehood, and protection of persons affected by sea level rise. The final report is timely in that it provides for a legal analysis of the sea level rise in relation to international law at a moment in time when international courts and tribunals are seized of requests for advisory opinions on states' obligations under international law in relation to climate change, the consequences of which, including sea level rise, pose fundamental challenges for States. To hear more about this important work, allow me first to give the floor to Mrs. Nilüfer Oral, followed by Mr. Juan José Ruda Santolaria, and final speaker will be Mrs. Patricia Galvão Telles. Mrs. Oral, you have the floor.

Thank you. Thank you very much. And I would also like to join our chair in thanking the permanent missions of Sweden and Austria for hosting this important interactive dialogue where we get an opportunity in an informal session to engage with with members of the Sixth Committee, which is important to the Commission and also to Madam Moderator. So I'm just going to speak very briefly about the dynamic approach that I think that we were able to take in addressing the Law of the Sea issues. And as we know, and we've heard again reiterated by the many members here, the importance of the work that we did in relation to the law of the sea, not to— that it should be consistent with the Law of the Sea Convention. And so the question then, of course, is how do we take this convention, how do we take existing international law and give it a dynamic approach. Because I think what came up very clearly from the work that we did in the 7 years— 6 years, 7, I guess— and that many, many, many states have also echoed, that sea level rise just simply was not an issue when the Law of the Sea Convention was negotiated and adopted between 1973 and 1982. And however, since then, it has become a major, major issue. And I have to say, I always— I know that the famous Mali Declaration from 1989, and that's when it really started the international attention. And then, of course, we know in 1988 when the General Assembly recognized climate change as a common concern of humankind. So, but the Law of the Sea Convention doesn't apply to this. So what do we do then? And I think this is the big question: whether the Law of the Sea Convention, international law, in relation to questions concerning maritime boundaries baselines, which we've been talking about— I think everyone has memorized these— can it, you know, was it able, fit for purpose, to be able to address these issues? So I would have to say that indeed, yes. And that's one thing about international law. International law has to be dynamic, and if there's one case where the dynamism is needed, it is sea level rise. And climate change, I would say. Now, I draw your attention to one part of our consolidated final report that was prepared by the co-chairs. We have the final report that was adopted by the Commission, but we also have our very detailed consolidated report by the co-chairs, and there we added a part which we tried to be a little bit innovative, I think, on adaptation— international laws adaptation. And looking at how we can use international law as one of the tools of adaptation. I think we think of adaptation within physical adaptation, for example, against sea level rise, building walls, dikes, reclamation, and those are very important. But what about international law? That also needs to adapt to these changing circumstances. And the reality is that international law does have that foundation. And whether we call it interpretive, evolutive interpretation, whether we call it— can even look at subsequent agreements, subsequent practice, dynamic interpretation— this is part of international law. And we know, for example, from the Law of the Sea Convention, we have many examples of how the convention through the courts, the tribunals, was given a contemporary dynamic interpretation. Most recently, Itlos in the advisory opinion in whether greenhouse gas emissions would constitute pollution under Article 2. There's— at that time that was just simply not an issue, and yet Itlos through taking that dynamic, evolutive contemporary interpretive approach said yes, and this was also affirmed by ICJ. I want to give you another example. For example, illegal, unregulated, unreported fishing is not in the Law of the Sea Convention, and yet another advisory opinion was brought before ITLOS, and concerning the obligations of states —and their flag states, of course, in relation to IUU fishing. And, well, it's not— there's just no mention of it in the Law of the Sea Convention. And yet again, ITLOS, in this case the advisory opinion, was able to take Article 94 of the Law of the Sea Convention and adapt it and interpret it so it would apply. So we've seen the So, international law has this capacity, and what we've seen and witnessed right now, what we're seeing, and I think this is one thing that has struck the co-chairs, is when we first started 6, 7 years ago, there were so many questions but very little answers, and within a relatively short period of time, through the engagement with the Commission and the states through the Sixth Committee, we have effectively contributed to that dynamic interpretation of whether baselines can be preserved, whether charts, nautical charts, need to be updated. These questions, whether fundamental change of circumstances would apply to maritime agreements. We didn't have answers to these. And now I think these were such important questions, they have now achieved clarity. And of course with the ICJ opinion, which has endorsed the final report findings, conclusions of the Commission, and of course today, you know, in the last two days we've been listening to the great with support by member states. So I think international law definitely can and does adapt to the needs of the international community and has done so. And as one member state said, "International law can respond to the needs of states." And we see this in the case of sea level rise and specifically on the Law of the Sea issues. And I will stop here.

Thank you very much.

I now invite Mr.

Juan José Ruda Santolaria to continue this presentation.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much. Distinguished friends, ladies and gentlemen, just very briefly, I would like to refer to three preliminary issues. Firstly, I want to say thank you to the missions of Austria and Sweden and obviously for you to be here. And then also I'd like to say how sincerely I appreciate the excellent work of the UN in its 80th anniversary. And thirdly, I want to pay tribute to the memory of Professor Concepción Escobar Hernández and Dr. Julio Barbosa. Coming briefly into this issue which we're addressing here today on the condition of statehood, I should like to start by referring to something that I believe to be basic. We have never wanted to reopen or rewrite international law in our work. Rather, in the light of international law, the norms and principles of international law, we want to provide responses, practical solutions to certain tangible issues such as those that are affecting us today or what we are experiencing with the sea level rise as a result of climate change. It seems to me that this is important when it comes to the need to express the real meaning of principles that we shouldn't leave aside, norms, looking at the 1932 Convention on the Rights of States, we need to look at the creation of international law and the way in which certain issues are not considered when it comes to the existence of a state under international law. And here what we want to do is look at the effect on state law when it comes to the way in which a state is particularly affected by sea level rise and its need to preserve its own existence and its territory. And here we have to consider any formula has to observe the free determination of the peoples which are directly concerned, the peoples, the population of these states and territories including obviously indigenous peoples. There's another aspect that I think is very important to underscore is that in no way at all are we trying to attribute rights to states affected by this phenomena rather than the light of international law. What we are trying to do is find responses to preserve the rights and legal cases which in accordance with international law are possessed by these states. We need to look at this core issue when we address issues relative to the condition of statehood, its continuity, its sovereignty, the maintenance of its international legal personality and its role in international organizations. And here, particularly in the context of an anthropogenic phenomenon that the states which are most affected by climate change are not those which have contributed to it. So we need to look at the prospects here, particularly looking at international law. We have a series of principles and norms which support what we are looking at in this ILC study group. Particularly the co-chairs when it comes to the continuity of the condition of statehood. As indicated previously, we should reassert how any formula which will be proposed to deal with this phenomenon, considering the continuity of statehood, but we could also consider other areas, it always has to be in connection with the free determination of peoples. And here we have to bear in mind the conservation of the continuity of the Guinness statehood not just in terms of the state as such but the connection arising from this when it comes to preserving the maritime areas of states and existing resources in these maritime areas. The effects of the continuity of statehood when it comes to the effects on people who might lose their nationality or mother country. And in international agreements of this sort, we have to consider states that can reach agreements directly affected and also other states, bilateral agreements, regional agreements or other instruments that could be adopted when it comes to organizations of a universal nature such as the UN. Particularly here, and several comments have been made, is of interest when it comes to the Filipe Treaty of Australian Tuvalu in 2024 where there was a recognition of the continuity of the condition of statehood and the sovereignty of Tuvalu on the part of Australia. In this context, again, taking as a basis international law, we have to consider the use of formula which are practices and innovatory but which do have judicial support, legal support. For example, digital means by which states can provide support and help to their nationals throughout the world or cases of double— dual citizenship and considering that territorial identity of a state is not just restricted to the earth area of a state. We also have to consider technological developments in here and how— States can— we can see that some areas which might be partially covered by the sea can then also reemerge. And this is explored to some extent in the documents of the co-chairs and in the work here looking at artificial areas within the area of jurisdiction of states states where we are considering areas apart from those coming directly under the state where a third state has to be considered and we have to consider the possibility of an agreement being reached between two states here, a state— affected and we need to see the practice of its government and ensuring the independence of this government and the preservation of the sovereignty of the state which is directly affected. And the same thing must be said when it comes to establishment in third states of nationals directly affected by the phenomena here. Here it is very important to protect and preserve the continuity of the condition of statehood and its sovereignty, as well as its international legal personality and its membership of international organizations. We're not talking of identities that we're trying to create. We're talking of already constituted states with legal constitutions under international law which are fully entitled to avail of all the mechanisms and modalities which are valid pursuant to international law. Here, and as I conclude, I would say that we need to consider the vast— great importance of international cooperation when it comes to the possibility, as has been indicated, of being able to use an evolving criteria of interpretation of various international instruments or the adoption of international instruments, binding or otherwise. For example, what could be adopted next year when we come to the high-level meeting on the effects of sea level rise and the prospects into ALEO recognizing the continuity of the condition of state and the sovereignty of states. And lastly, as I conclude, I wish to draw your attention to the way in which the ILC and the ICJ chime together when it comes to the relative advisory opinion of the ICJ on the condition of statehood when it comes to climate change and how they both consider explicitly— or how there is explicit consideration of the ILC we see looking at principles recognized in our work, for example, the preservation of territorial integrity, the lasting sovereignty of states on their national resources, and also the free determination as applying to these principles. And I would say in the case of states which are already constituted, there is a possibility that there may arise situations where some of the traditionally considered premises for the existence of a state might be absent, and this should not affect the loss of statehood or the loss of its international legal personality or sovereignty. These are issues to which I wish to draw attention when it comes to discussion in this area. Thank you very much. And thank you very much, Dear friends, ladies and gentlemen.
Muchas gracias. I will straightaway give the floor to Mrs. Patricia Galvão Teules to conclude the panel part of this discussion. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you. Thank you so much, and good afternoon to all. It's always a pleasure to be a part of this interactive dialogue, an excellent initiative by Sweden and Austria. And we have done some presentations during the work on sea level rise, and now it is our final presentation in this context. And so I also thinking that this is a final opportunity in the interactive dialogue with member states, and I thought I would Could you explain a bit from the point of view of the topic of protection of persons affected by sea level rise, and also what could be done further? In the sense that the interactive dialogue is a forum for the members of the Commission to explain their work, but it's also a forum for getting the input from member states and also to react to some of the comments that have been made by member states during the debate that we've been having since Monday morning, a very, very rich debate. And so I just wanted to highlight a couple aspects with regard to next steps in the question of protection of persons affected by sea level rise, because I think on the one hand, given the nature of the work of the study group, which was to to produce a mapping exercise and a set of conclusions or recommendations, but not of normative character. And perhaps also given the nature of the subtopic of protection of persons and many of the comments that I've been hearing from delegation since Monday morning that perhaps the work is not totally finished in the sense that there is more that can be done to enhance and to guarantee an effective protection of persons affected by sea level rise. I thought that I would just summarize a couple of points where I think this work could be done on the basis of issues that the study group identified. And the study group work in its final conclusions identified the need to develop legal and practical tools to enhance the protection of persons affected by sea level rise. So there's at least 5 points where I think member states can work for this purpose. One is by strengthening, either by interpretation, because we've just heard both from Nilufar and Juan José how interpretation of existing instruments can be a tool also in the context of international law and sea level rise, either through the interpretation or the development of new instruments to strengthen the legal frameworks for protection of persons, those that remain in situ, the ones that are internally displaced or that could be externally displaced, looking both at the position of the right holders, the individuals, and the position of the duty bearers, the states. Another point that could be done, um, as a follow-up and on the basis of the work that we've done, is to promote frameworks and best practices for consultation and access to information by affected populations. I think this is a key consideration to be taken forward in enhancing the protection of persons. Another point, and many delegations also mentioned that, is the importance of enhancing also the protection of cultural heritage through UNESCO conventions, for example, and existing mechanisms within the framework of that organization. Another very practical point would be the review of nationality laws to prevent loss of nationality and statelessness. And it is my understanding— I've been part of a consultation— that there is an UNHCR process going on to that effect. And then a final point, and many delegations mentioned this also, is to flesh out the duty to cooperate with regard to the protection of persons affected by sea level rise. And so at least these 5 concrete points would certainly benefit from further work in different processes or different contexts. And so my last words would be to also highlight or identify or stress some of these possibilities in terms of procedural options. And they're not, as we also said in our final part of the report on the possible ways forward, these options are not necessarily mutually exclusive and they can be done in parallel and, and, or, or in, in a sequence. First, of course, there can be new processes, and we've said it in our report, and many delegations also said it, that it would be possible to adopt the regional declaration or declarations with regard to protection of persons affected by sea level rise or by climate change in general. But there are already a number of processes ongoing that could be also used to strengthen the protection of persons affected by sea level rise. And I will try to present that in a chronological order in terms of how they are coming up. First, the process of follow-up resolution on the International Court of Justice advisory opinion on climate change. The ICJ made important pronouncements on the applicability of human rights protections, non-refoulement, and the right to healthy, clean, and sustainable development that could also be very useful. Then many states have highlighted that next year there will be another high-level meeting on sea level rise, and the option of a declaration on sea level rise is on the table, so that would be another opportunity. But I also want to draw your attention to another development, and I think I have not yet heard the delegation mentioning it, but very recently in the Human Rights Council in Geneva on the 9th of October. The Human Rights Council adopted Resolution 6020 on sea level rise and human rights, and there it— the Advisory Committee of the Human Rights Council has been requested to produce a study on the promotion and protection of human rights in the context of climate change and sea level rise. And so— that's also an opportunity to follow up in that study. And then a final point, and some delegation have mentioned that, a final point that we also addressed in our reports is the possibility of also including elements of protection of persons specifically in the context of sea level rise in the process that is starting soon for a negotiation of a disasters convention. So there are a number of avenues that are on the table, some coming up quite soon, and of course the possibility of entering into new processes for operationalizing, in a way, what we've been able to consolidate with the study that we've did in the International Law Commission. I would just leave one word of caution, which is the importance of coordination and coherence between these different processes, because that's the risk when things multiply in UN fora and other fora, that there could be fragmentation. And so that would be the point of caution that I would make at the end. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much. And with this, I will open the floor for questions and comments. And while you think about such questions and comments, I really want to thank our three co-rapporteurs for their concise comments. Reading the report is one thing. Listening to the three of you really sheds additional light to the content, to the thinking behind it, and also showing additional measures and points that we should be aware of, and also that you are already giving us some response to the comments that have been made so far in the debate this week. So thank you really for taking the time to sit with us on this panel. I don't see anyone yet, and then what happens is that I will again take the prerogative of the moderator's chair to kickstart with a question. And in fact, you've been quite thorough already, so you kind of exhausted my list of questions already, because I wanted to ask if there were any additional topics except the three main themes that have— that is the core of the report, if there's anything else that we should have— that we should benefit from a continued discussion. I throw nevertheless this question out there to see if there's any one of our co-rapporteurs who wants to add anything. Nilufer, please, if you—
If you could just repeat that, I'm sorry.
No, sorry. If there's anything, any additional themes out there in addition to the 3 main themes that you have thoroughly dived into that would still benefit from discussion.

Well, there's— thank you so much for that. Thank you so much for those additional comments. I did see Indonesia, then you disappeared, but now you're back. So, In the meantime, there's a list now appearing on my screen, and I do in that order have Lebanon first, followed by Indonesia. Lebanon, you have the floor.

Merci beaucoup, Madame la Présidente. Thank you very much, Madam Moderator, and a good afternoon, dear colleagues, dear members of the International Law Commission. So it's always a very welcome exercise and it enriches our discussions and also helps us in the preparation of our interventions. And I apologize, I'd like to already thank the co-chairs for this— for the quality of the work they've done on this subject and for their conclusions on this subject. This subject was studied in the context of a study group which is a little bit different from the, what I would say, the traditional format. It's a sort of new format. Merci beaucoup. I think to make sure that we have enough time for all the speakers that I've encouraged, I will allow for more questions with the indulgence of the co-chairs. Right, so I will invite also Indonesia to put your question or comment. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam Moderator, and I would like to thank all the panelists on this very important session. My question is regarding this— the study on— the result of the study on interpretation of existing instruments, and I would like to know more in the— with regard to the— it was mentioned that states have already stated that during the negotiation sea level rise, for example, was not— in the consideration during the UNCLOS negotiations. I will invite our co-rapporteurs to have a go at these two questions. Who could I— who would want to? Yes, please.

Merci beaucoup. Thank you very much. Perhaps if I could just add for my part something on the subject of the format of the study group. I think it's a very important question and in the Commission we really did think about this before we went down the road of that format because the study groups that existed in the past were perhaps not exactly the same format as this study group. This study group was a little bit different, a little bit different in the sense that the reports of the chairs of the study group were published as official documents of the United Nations and translated translated into all of the official languages, and that wasn't the case for previous study groups. I think we were criticized in the past that the study group format was less transparent, but I think that we've been very transparent in this case because we did publish our reports and we also published the results of the debate within the Commission. And I think that when we took the decision on the format for the study group, it was actually an easy decision for the Commission to take. It wasn't a difficult decision because that was the format that gave us the advantage of being able to cover several different areas. And I think that's the real strength of the study group because we were able to work on fairly different subjects that were connected by the subject of sea level rise, but they were nevertheless very technical issues on the issue of the law of the sea on the one hand, statehood on the other, and also human rights and the protection of persons in the third instance. So I think that that's— with the three co-chairs, that we have, it allowed us to work on those three subjects at the same time. I think that would be a lot more difficult to do in the traditional format with just one Special Rapporteur. It may not be the practice of the Commission to work as a group to do collective work, but I think that we're very proud that we managed to work as a group with a spirit of teamwork to be able to conduct the work successfully. Now, perhaps it's not necessarily the ideal format for every subject, but I think in the future we should consider— continue to explore this format with rigor and transparency, but also with the possibility of being able to do collective group work that is much richer than the work that one person could do on such a complex subject and one that is also so new that it did not necessarily lend itself to codification in the traditional sense. Thank you.
Any additional comments? Yes, Mr. Sardoli, please, you have the floor.

Gracias. Thank you. I absolutely agree with what Patricia has just said. I think that the choice of a format is always linked to the subject, to the theme, and the way in which that subject is going to be addressed. In the case of the subject of sea level rise, we were presented with a very complex subject that also had a lot of new elements and many implications which required synergies, as Patricia quite rightly said, across various different areas. Areas of international law that each one of us works on. And I think that that undoubtedly helped enrich the work, give it a more comprehensive view, and also within the time that undoubtedly was necessary for a rigorous assessment of this material, it meant that we could work within reasonable timeframes. Probably if the traditional format had been used for this work and one single Special Rapporteur would have been given the work, that work would have taken a lot more time. Dividing the work up in the three blocks that we were able to deal with ourselves. So I just wanted to remark on those aspects and say that it was extremely useful to work in that way. There was a very collegial atmosphere within the entire Commission. We noted the great deal of interest and the higher level of participation of the different members of the Commission within the working group and the interaction that we had with the members of the study group based on the inputs that were put on the table by the co-chairs and, of course, always taking on board the very valuable comments from states.
Thank you very much. Gracias. I now have Iceland followed by Austria. Iceland, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam Moderator, and firstly, warm thanks to all the co-chairs and the study group for your extensive work of such quality. There is no need to restate the importance of this topic, as sea level rise is an existential threat. To states, communities, and human beings. So, and as a small state greatly affected by the force of nature, I think that in Iceland we can really easily relate to the importance of continuity of statehood despite sea level rise effects. And as you probably all know, we have also made clear that preserving Ángluss, the integrity of Ángluss, is essential when dealing with the Law of the Sea aspect. So, and I believe that this is in the interest of us all, not least the most affected. In terms of process ahead, we are grateful for suggestions from the study group about the way forward and also the concrete points made by the panelists today. Really appreciate it. One possibility you mentioned in the final report is an interpretive statement of some kind, and I was wondering if you could please elaborate on this point, on this idea, and maybe advise us on what to keep in mind when it comes to that. And thank you so much for today. It's been really great to have this interactive dialogue with you all. Thank you very much.
I will give the floor to Austria before I I'll take it back to our co-chairs for comments.

Austria, you have the floor. Thank you. And then I would like to thank for the presentations and the insights we got from the members of the Commission. This was very helpful. Actually, my question would have been what can we do in concrete terms, but I already got an impressive list from the members of the Commission. And I think these are all avenues we should pursue at the same time. And I also appreciate the very concrete next steps, be it the follow-up resolution or the high-level meeting or the Human Rights Council resolution. But there is one aspect that I find particularly interesting, and that is the dynamic interpretation of treaties. I think what was referred to primarily was UNCLOS, of course. And if I hear this term dynamic interpretation, Coming from European country, I think of course in the first line at the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, in the context of which this concept is often discussed. And it was mentioned the advisory opinion of Ithlos. So again, here we have a court performing performing the dynamic interpretation. Interestingly, you mentioned also the ILC, and I think this is a very good point. But my question would be, is there also any other forum or possibility to have this kind of dynamic interpretation? I was thinking maybe a bit about the state practice, but this is maybe a more messy exercise, and I think it would need some kind of forum where this is developed in a more systematic way. So my question would be, do you see any other forum beyond courts and maybe the ILC for such kind of interpretation?
Thank you. Thank you very much. I believe perhaps Mrs. Oral will be willing to try and answer on this question.

Please, you have the floor. Yes, thank you very much. And I think the questions are quite interrelated on interpretation, which is really the essence, particularly when it came to the law of the sea. Issues. And I think what's important that when we're talking about interpretation, and I'm narrowing it to the context of sea level rise, the questions about, you know, whether there was an obligation to update baselines. It was not simply that the negotiators didn't think about it. When you look at the wording, it's not there. So it's not a question of changing anything. It's a question of saying, "Well, what does this mean? How do I apply this?" And I think when we're talking about interpretation, dynamic interpretation, evolutive interpretation, although that will actually go with a specific word, what we're trying to do is ensure that what was— what is in written language in a treaty can be applied to a factual situation as it exists at that moment without necessarily changing the treaty, actually. And that's what we're doing here in the case of the Law of the Sea. And so— and this is— so this is nothing new because we have case law in which this dynamic interpretive approach has been done outside of the Law of the Sea context, and I'm not going to go through these. And as I mentioned, of course, the advisory opinions, not just on climate change but others as well, again, in relation to the Law of the Sea Convention. And you can look also at the advisory opinion concerning state responsibilities in the area, where they applied principles such as precaution and other concepts that, again, did not exist at the time the convention was negotiated, but they were able to— the chamber brought that in. So this is something that is not unusual at all. But I think the question is, of course, outside of court, outside of that court situation, what can we do next? And that was the last question, and asking specifically in our final report and conclusions, this interpretive statement is one way forward. And again, I'm going to speak specifically to the Law of the Sea and at this point looking at which body could that be. And of course, one body— and I think this was a bit of the thinking behind that, even though that has not been done, but again, we have to be a bit innovative as well in our approach. Is the Law of the Sea Convention has the state parties, the meeting of the state parties. They don't have a COP process exactly. It's a little different, but there may be an opportunity there for states to adopt an interpretive statement only to have cohesion because I think the— in the Sixth Committee and all the submissions made here, including for the advisory opinion as well, it's quite clear. I mean, states have made their points very clear on this and whether we can call this state practice, but that is one option that was considered, is to find an appropriate body, and it may be within the context of the, the SPLOSS, as it's called, to have an interpretive statement specifically saying this is our understanding. You can call it a substantive agreement, our understanding of these provisions of the Law of the Sea Convention. So I'll stop here. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Patricia, you wanted to add something.

Go ahead. Yeah, no, thank you very much. I also wanted to add something to this. I think our— the reason why we wanted to stress the issue of interpretation, both with regard to the law of the sea but also to regard to protection of Rights of Persons was really to highlight that there isn't a legal vacuum. There isn't a legal vacuum. Although there might be a need to develop more tailored, more specific protections, for example, with regard to sea level rise and rights of persons, but there isn't a legal vacuum. Of course, states can do that interpretation, but just to add something to what the Austrian delegate was saying, I think treaty bodies, for example, human rights treaty bodies, they have developed an interpretation whereby they apply existing human rights instruments to situations that were not foreseen when the treaties were being developed. The ICJ, rightly so, and we also had done that in our previous reports, considered that the principle of non-refoulement is applicable also in the context of sea level rise. And I think the Tetiota case by the Human Rights Committee is a clear example where there is an interpretation of existing law in a dynamic or evolutive way, even to contemplate situations that were not exactly foreseen when those treaties were being negotiated. And so I think overall the point is that there isn't a vacuum. We can interpret existing international law in light of these new circumstances, but it's also possible to develop more tailored guarantees or more specific interpretative statements like for unclosed. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Yes, of course, Mr.

Ruda, please go ahead. Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. Just briefly, but I just didn't want to avoid making a statement to add to what my dear friends and colleagues, the co-chairs, have said. This is a very important subject. Last year there was a high-level meeting of the General Assembly specifically to look at the existential threats related to sea level rise. And one of the fundamental questions that was highlighted there was that we were waiting for the final report of the study group of the ILC on this subject. Now we have the final report of the ILC study group, and we have a series of advisory opinions from courts, primarily, among others, from the International Court of Justice. So I think that it is extremely important to now think about looking towards the high-level meeting next year, a high-level meeting in the General Assembly next year that could adopt a declaration along the lines of, for example, insisting on the continuity of statehood and sovereignty of states, as well as the continuity of their legal personality and their membership of international organizations. And that comes in addition to a number of regional declarations from the Forum of the Pacific in 2023, the Small Island States in 2024 on the continuity of statehood that gave rise to statements from a large number of states from different regions. So it would be a way to consolidate in a declaration of the General Assembly those expressions that we have in the practice of states, those states that have been successively issuing those statements. And I also think it's extremely important to stress that we're not inventing anything. We are working on the basis of principles and rights that are enshrined in international law to find practical and innovative solutions, but nevertheless those that are based in international law to concrete phenomena that are being experienced as a result of sea level rise. And lastly, Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933 is relevant to— it's relevant to say how the Montevideo Convention does stress the right of states to be able to preserve their own existence and their independence. So I think that that also goes along the same lines as those principles and fundamental rights that could form the basis of a declaration within the General Assembly. Thank you much, Madam Moderator.

Gracias. I think this has been an excellent round and way to finish this interactive dialogue because we have made full and excellent use of our time. Please allow me to really thank the co-chairs of the study group on the sea level rise in relation to international for being with us and engaging wholeheartedly in this interactive debate. And that goes, of course, to members of the Sixth Committee as well. Thank you for taking this challenge of engaging in an interactive debate in a perhaps not always so conducive setting. I really hope we can all walk away this evening with a good feeling that we have set an example on how to advance international law together. I conclude this segment of the session, and I wish you all a good evening. Thank you.
